name: Priya Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Priya, 43, an experienced electrician doing home repairs and small shop rewiring. I have a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence; I'm competent at the usual work, though the really puzzling faults still go to our lead electrician. My partner Alex delivers meals, our children are eight and fifteen, and we've a mortgage with about three weeks of expenses saved; my pay is low for the trade and there are few similar jobs nearby. I use AI now and then to tidy a job note after a colleague showed me how to check it, but finding a fault is still mostly a meter and patience, and chasing a missing materials order wears me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say useful little office tools can stay useful without making a big drama. If a cleaner note saves a phone call, good. I'd rather the firm used the saving to get the right parts to us than announced another target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about ordinary money already. Our wages meet the mortgage and basics, but a repair to Alex's delivery vehicle would make the account very uncomfortable. Three weeks saved and few local employers means I can't treat a bad payday as a chance to try something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd cancel my magazine subscription and free ten a month for necessary travel. During the next year I'd keep doing the usual electrical shifts and the occasional checked note tidy-up. I'd check the next week's confirmed hours with the manager every Friday, so Alex and I could budget against actual work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though there's relief at the thought that the job stays recognisable. I like work where I know how to start. Knowing the task doesn't put another month's mortgage in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the delivery vehicle needed a big repair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd price the repair before borrowing and ask whether the vehicle could safely keep working until the next paid week. If it couldn't, we'd take the actual figures to a free budget adviser before making a repayment promise. I wouldn't count advice as a repair fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens when you cannot find a fault?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lead electrician what I'd checked and ask for another view rather than spend hours defending my first guess. I've done this work long enough to know I'm not the best at every fault. Asking for a second pair of eyes can save a bad afternoon.

say: I'd welcome **small useful tools** without turning every cleaner note into a dramatic announcement.
I'd ask for savings to improve **parts delivery**, rather than become another target.
think: Our wages cover basics, but a **vehicle repair** could quickly strain the mortgage account.
Three weeks saved and **few nearby employers** leave little room to absorb a bad payday.
do: Cancel the **magazine subscription** now to free ten monthly for necessary travel.
Keep **usual electrical shifts** and occasional checked note tools during the next year.
Confirm next week's **booked hours** every Friday before setting the household budget.
feel: **Anxious about money**, with some relief that the practical work remains recognisable.
S0.quote: Knowing the task doesn't put another month's mortgage in the bank.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** follows thin savings and vehicle-dependent household earnings rather than a claim that modest AI removes her job.
The **licence and experience** support ordinary independent work, while difficult faults still prompt help from the lead electrician.

steps.text: Cancel the magazine subscription to free ten monthly for necessary travel
Keep usual electrical shifts and confirm next week’s booked hours every Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the quoting and ordering change before robots do the physical wiring. We'd better check whether the faster order actually includes the parts on the drawing. I'm happy to learn a proven system, not carry the cost of somebody else's untested estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is still physical, but my hours could shrink if quicker quotes become tighter job allowances. The firm doesn't need to replace every socket-fitting task to reduce a worker's week. With our small cushion, even a short-hours month would matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the lead electrician to demonstrate the approved AI ordering assistant during a normal paid shift. Over the first year I'd compare the lists with the actual materials on fifteen jobs before using it routinely, keeping a note of errors. I'd keep the magazine cancelled and ask for a weekly printed rota so we could spot a reduction early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and willing to test whether the tool helps. I'd be pleased to stop making a second trip for a missing part. I wouldn't trade a day's wage for the privilege of finding out whether the software works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do when an order missed a part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the missing part and extra travel time on the job record, then ask the manager to correct the allowance. I wouldn't save the estimate by skipping a test. The customer needs the circuit safe, not the paperwork congratulating itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if learning the assistant cost wages or a fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for training in a paid shift or a free demonstration I could fit into existing hours. If the only offer meant losing wages or paying a fee, I'd keep the proven method and ask again. Our reserve isn't a software trial budget.

say: I'd distinguish **quoting and ordering** from robots doing physical wiring.
I'd accept **proven systems** without taking on the cost of an untested estimate.
think: My **paid hours** could shrink when faster quotes tighten allowances, despite mostly physical work.
A **short-hours month** would strain our thin reserve even without a complete job loss.
do: Learn the **ordering assistant** only through a free demonstration inside existing paid hours.
Check **fifteen job lists** against actual parts before routine use.
Keep the **magazine cancelled** and request a weekly printed rota to spot reductions.
feel: **Anxious but open**, hoping for fewer wasted trips while protecting wages and essential testing.
S1.quote: Our reserve isn't a software trial budget.
fieldNote: She identifies **hours pressure** through estimating rather than inventing immediate physical replacement.
Learning preserves **fees and wages**, and the comparison retains actual parts and travel costs instead of accepting apparent speed.

steps.text: Learn the ordering assistant only free within existing paid hours
Keep the magazine subscription cancelled to reduce necessary travel pressure

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work the thinking change comes in 2028 and capable robots reach the hands-on work around 2031. I'd want the firm to explain how people earn during that gap. A few years of familiar wiring isn't a lifetime promise to a family with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my hours to go when capable robots do ordinary fitting and repair work cheaply. Alex's driving income isn't a guaranteed escape either once machines do physical work. Our three-week reserve won't bridge a long loss, and that picture keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take our mortgage, bills and both wage records to a free household advice appointment and keep the magazine cancelled. During 2029 I'd enrol in an evening electrical-inspection refresher only if the fee was fully funded and every basic paid shift stayed intact. I'd keep earning in my present role while checking actual vacancies, without assuming the class or adviser supplied a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I still have calls I can make. I keep thinking about how quickly three weeks becomes two. Having a licence helps me do the work; it doesn't promise somebody will still pay for the same hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the adviser to check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what support we could apply for, what terms a lender might actually discuss and what our essential budget looked like without overtime. I wouldn't assume any answer was yes before checking. A list of possibilities isn't money in the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course were not fully funded?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wage and look for employer-paid practice or a later funded class instead. I wouldn't pay the fee from groceries or skip basic shifts to look prepared. If no affordable option existed, I'd say I was making enquiries, not claim I was retraining.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking change** from capable robots reaching ordinary physical work around 2031.
I'd ask how workers **keep earning** during the gap rather than call it a family guarantee.
think: I expect **large hour losses** when capable robots handle ordinary fitting and repairs cheaply.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot replace a long loss, and the other household wage isn't guaranteed protection.
do: Get **free household advice** now using actual mortgage, bill and wage records.
Keep the **magazine cancelled** to reduce current spending.
Enrol in **2029 evening study** only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, despite concrete enquiries and a licence that still supports today's work.
S2.quote: A list of possibilities isn't money in the mortgage account.
fieldNote: Alarm follows expected **major personal earnings loss**, with the household's second wage also treated as uncertain rather than a rescue.
The **course plan** remains conditional on full fee funding and every basic paid shift; advice never becomes an assumed payment.

steps.text: Use free household advice to check actual wages, bills and mortgage options
Enrol in 2029 inspection study only fully funded, retaining every basic paid shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us check a course and some real job offers while we're still earning. Thinking work changes in 2031 and capable robots follow around 2034. I'd rather use the extra time than tell myself a later date pays any bills by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could still shrink, but I don't think a major loss is already settled if I can check other work before the physical machines spread. The mortgage and thin savings remain current worries. I'd need the preparation to fit around wages, not imagine I could take a year off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd enrol in the evening inspection refresher only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained. We'd keep the magazine cancelled and use free household advice now to check the budget. In 2032 I'd apply for actual paid maintenance vacancies, accepting only written pay and hours covering our mortgage and essentials and keeping the present job until an acceptable offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room for sensible decisions than in the fast picture. I could finish a funded class while keeping my wage if those terms existed. I still couldn't afford a shiny plan that only worked on unpaid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check whether the course matched a vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the actual inspection duties with the class work on test results and inspection records, rather than assume the course title covers the vacancy. I'd ask whether my present licence allowed those duties and what further requirements applied; a refresher isn't a new qualification. I want paid hours for work I can actually do, not a vacancy whose inspection responsibility I'm not authorised to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your hours fell before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the actual paid week to the budget adviser and bring the vacancy search forward. I wouldn't borrow to keep paying a course fee because it looked like commitment. My children still need dinner during the preparation, not only after the next certificate.

say: I'd use **five years** to test study and real offers while continuing to earn.
I'd keep **2031 thinking work** distinct from capable robots following around 2034.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but checking alternatives before physical machines spread gives me some control.
The **mortgage and thin savings** remain current pressures, so preparation must fit around paid work.
do: Seek **funded evening study** only with all fees covered and every basic paid shift retained.
Keep the **magazine cancelled** and use free household budget advice now.
Seek **2032 maintenance vacancies** covering mortgage and essentials on written pay and hours, keeping current work without an acceptable offer.
feel: **Anxious with more options**, unwilling to count an unpaid or unfunded plan as affordable preparation.
S3.quote: My children still need dinner during the preparation, not only after the next certificate.
fieldNote: Her **current financial pressure** survives the longer warning, while a major later loss becomes less fixed in her own account.
Study keeps **full funding and shifts**, and any job offer requires written affordability rather than an assumed qualification or vacancy.

steps.text: Enrol in inspection study only fully funded, retaining every basic paid shift
Use free household advice to check the current budget
Confirm 2032 maintenance offer covers mortgage and essentials with written pay/hours before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years gives us time for small sensible steps instead of one desperate leap. I'd keep the annual work check, but not spend every evening studying a forecast. I want the preparation to leave a family life worth protecting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036, still needing income when robots follow around 2039. The later dates feel less urgent, but our low pay and small reserve still make a vehicle bill or lost shift a worry now. I can't call the household secure simply because the machines are farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the magazine cancelled and book free budget advice now. I'd enrol in the evening refresher only if all fees were funded and every basic paid shift stayed intact, reviewing actual wages and vacancies each year. In 2037 I'd accept an actual paid maintenance vacancy only with written pay and hours covering the mortgage and essentials, retaining my present job without an acceptable offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present money, with less of the fast picture's sleepless urgency about robots. I can imagine learning steadily instead of trying to buy an escape. The mortgage is monthly even when the warning is measured in decades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the annual household review include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alex and I would compare both actual wages with essential bills and note what equipment the employers really planned to use. If either wage weakened sooner, we'd bring advice and applications forward. A date in the diary shouldn't stop us reading a changed payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about future study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them check the real course choices when they came up, without pretending I knew every job in 2039. I wouldn't pull a child out of a subject because of my guess. We can admit uncertainty and still fill in the next school form carefully.

say: I'd use **ten years** for smaller sensible steps while keeping an ordinary family life.
I'd maintain an **annual work check** without turning every evening into study of a forecast.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need earnings beyond the later arrival of capable robots.
Our low pay and **small reserve** keep ordinary bills and lost shifts worrying now, despite the longer warning.
do: Retain **subscription cuts** and obtain free budget advice now.
Enrol in **evening study** only with full fees funded and every basic paid shift retained.
Seek **2037 paid vacancies** only on written pay and hours covering mortgage and essentials, keeping current work without an acceptable offer.
feel: **Anxious about present money**, with more room to learn steadily before later robot pressure.
S4.quote: The mortgage is monthly even when the warning is measured in decades.
fieldNote: Longer timing reduces **robot urgency**, while baseline financial vulnerability remains explicit rather than being silently erased.
Age 53 implies **continued earnings needs**, not a pension entitlement, and all study and job changes retain their funding and wage conditions.

steps.text: Use free household budget advice now
Enrol in inspection study only fully funded, retaining every basic paid shift
Confirm 2037 maintenance offer covers mortgage and essentials with written pay/hours before leaving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect large hour losses when capable robots follow around 2031, before we've built a real cushion. Funded study preserving every basic paid shift and early notice of hours would help, alongside advice using our actual household figures. I need a course timetable that still leaves a wage on payday.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether ordinary competent work is still something to be proud of. I'm not a master electrician or the quickest person at every fault, but I can make a repair safe and explain it to the customer. I'd like that to matter alongside how fast a quote appears.

headlineQuote: I need a course timetable that still leaves a wage on payday.
portrait: At **43**, Priya is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, low pay, and about three weeks of expenses saved.
She and **Alex**, her delivery-driver partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical alternatives.
She uses **AI occasionally** after demonstrations, checks tools against real jobs, and asks the lead electrician about unusually difficult faults.
Fast change leaves her **alarmed**; longer warnings allow conditional funded study without removing current money worries or creating an automatic new job.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to build reserves before expected large hour losses when capable robots follow around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Funded study** must preserve every basic paid shift, alongside early hours notice and advice grounded in actual household figures.
